articles.text: Piedmont’s 25th Annual Turkey Trot has finally arrived. This Thursday, November 26, thousands of local runners will do a 5K run through Piedmont’s streets. Currently, 2,194 participants have signed up for the race out of a total of 2,800. Turkey Trot organizer Sydney Proctor expects the race to sell out, with close to 600 spots remaining. The Turkey Trot starts at 8:30 a.m. at the Exedra on Highland and Magnolia avenues, but Proctor encourages runners to arrive 20 minutes early for parking and check-in. Race bibs can be picked up Wednesday, November 25, from 3 to 6 p.m. at Veterans Hall, or on race day from 7:45 to 8:15 a.m. Local organizations will collect donations of clothes, toys, books, and food at Wednesday’s pickup. The top finisher in each age group will receive a pie, and the top three will receive a bouquet. The top three finishers overall will receive sponsor gift cards. The top two finishers (male/ female) will get a turkey, a new pair of shoes, and a limited-edition Turkey Trot hat. Weather reports indicate that Thursday morning will be dry after days of rain caused by the El Niño storms. Organizers recommend runners prepare for the potential rain and bring their coats or umbrellas in case reports change. Continue to monitor the weather report to be prepared for any changes in conditions. The student-led Piedmont Service Crew will serve hot chocolate, coffee, and pies to runners, and the Turkey Trot will make matching donations to the group. The race supports Piedmont schools’ cross country and track & field programs along with other running clubs. Since 2017, the Piedmont Turkey Trot has successfully funneled $205,000 back into the local community, including $135,000 towards the Hampton Field rebuild. Registration is $59 for adults and children 13 and older. Registration for children 12 and under is $38. There is no same-day registration; runners must register ahead of time. articles.text: Grappling with how to stay connected when your kid is on the move? Some parents give their kids smartwatches to provide some autonomy while delaying access to the internet and social media. Internet-free smartwatches may be somewhat less “sticky” and distracting than larger-screened phones, and a device attached to the wrist is also less likely to be lost by active kids. According to my ten-year-old, Andreas, some of his fourth-grade buddies have smartwatches, but almost no kid his age has a smart phone. Since he turned 10, he has had an Apple Watch with limited apps and strong parental controls. “I like to be able to text and call my friends, and it’s fun counting my steps,” Andreas says. He often uses his watch to see if friends can meet to hang out – a communication loop I’m happy to be out of, giving him the same freedom to manage his social life that I had when I was a kid. I also like that he can update me when roaming the neighborhood with friends. But smartwatches come with downsides too: “I made the decision not to get my kids watches when I noticed a bunch of fourthgrade boys at a birthday party were looking at their watches and not interacting with each other,” says one Beach dad. Lack of games or extraneous apps on a watch can help prevent overuse, but texting can be mesmerizing, especially as kids learn to send funny photos and memes. Another caution: group chats can devolve into trouble. If you choose to give your child access to a device that enables group chats, make it clear they need to inform you immediately if the exchanges become hurtful to them or others, or if inappropriate material is being shared. Considerations in choosing a smartwatch Thinking about a smartwatch for your kid? The offerings in the kid-friendly smartwatch market are updated regularly, and you can consult outlets like NYT Wirecutter and Parents Magazine for comparisons. Common smartwatch models in Piedmont include the Apple Watch, the TickTalk, and the Gizmo. These key questions are a good starting point to consider in evaluating options: • The most important thing, from the perspective of Piedmont Unplugged parents: Does it adequately block (or simply not provide) unrestricted access to the internet and social media? • Does the device flag abusive texts or inappropriate content for parents? • Is it possible to circumvent the parental controls on the device (and how likely is my kid to do so)? Device-free is still the best choice for some families If you choose not to give your kid a portable digital device, you are far from alone. A Piedmont mom I know held strong against getting her seventh-grade daughter a phone or watch. She noted with pride that her daughter had become resourceful about finding the right adult to speak to when she needed assistance. “I told her to find a mom or a nanny, or in the center of town, to talk to someone working at Mulberry’s or a police officer.” Now, she says, her daughter is glad she doesn’t have a device because “I’m not brought into the crazy drama that is happening” among friends on group texts. “I used to think I would be uncool and missing out, but this year, I don’t care.” Amanda Straub is a co-founder of Piedmont Unplugged

articles.text: Not everything advertised as an “e-bike” is actually an electric bicycle under California law. Some are powerful electric motorcycles capable of traveling at much higher speeds than parents might expect. Even legal e-bikes can be fast and heavy. A child who isn’t prepared to handle a bike’s speed, weight, or acceleration can lose control, resulting in a crash that causes serious injury. Before purchasing an e-bike, the Piedmont Police Department urges parents to review the different types of e-bikes available and choose one appropriate for their child’s age, experience, and riding ability. California has three classes of e-bikes. Understanding the capabilities of each class can help you choose an appropriate bike for your child. • Class 1: Pedal assist, up to 20mph. The motor provides power only while the rider is pedaling. There is no minimum age requirement. • Class 2: Throttle assist, up to 20 mph. The motor can propel the bike without pedaling. There is no minimum age requirement. • Class 3: Pedal assist, up to 28 mph. These bikes provide motor assistance while pedaling at higher speeds. Riders must be at least 16 years old. All three classes must have working pedals and a motor that does not exceed 750 watts. Helmets are required for all riders under 18, and for Class 3 riders of any age. Just because a child is legally allowed to ride a particular class of e-bike doesn’t mean they’re ready to ride it safely. Consider their riding experience, judgment, and ability to control the bike. Before your child starts riding, make sure they have a properly fitted helmet and understand the rules of the road. Talk about riding at safe speeds, stopping at stop signs, yielding to pedestrians, and avoiding distractions like phones and earbuds. An e-bike can give teens greater independence and a convenient way to get around Piedmont. Choosing the right bike – and making sure your child knows how to ride it safely – can help them enjoy those benefits while reducing the risk of injury. For more information about e-bike classifications, age restrictions, and safe riding practices, visit the Piedmont Police Department’s e-bike and e-scooter safety guide for parents. He often uses his watch to see if friends can meet to hang out – a communication loop I’m happy to be out of, giving him the same freedom to manage his social life that I had when I was a kid. I also like that he can update me when roaming the neighborhood with friends. But smartwatches come with downsides too: “I made the decision not to get my kids watches when I noticed a bunch of fourthgrade boys at a birthday party were looking at their watches and not interacting with each other,” says one Beach dad. Lack of games or extraneous apps on a watch can help prevent overuse, but texting can be mesmerizing, especially as kids learn to send funny photos and memes. Another caution: group chats can devolve into trouble. If you choose to give your child access to a device that enables group chats, make it clear they need to inform you immediately if the exchanges become hurtful to them or others, or if inappropriate material is being shared. Considerations in choosing a smartwatch Thinking about a smartwatch for your kid? The offerings in the kid-friendly smartwatch market are updated regularly, and you can consult outlets like NYT Wirecutter and Parents Magazine for comparisons. Common smartwatch models in Piedmont include the Apple Watch, the TickTalk, and the Gizmo. These key questions are a good starting point to consider in evaluating options: • The most important thing, from the perspective of Piedmont Unplugged parents: Does it adequately block (or simply not provide) unrestricted access to the internet and social media? • Does the device flag abusive texts or inappropriate content for parents? • Is it possible to circumvent the parental controls on the device (and how likely is my kid to do so)? Device-free is still the best choice for some families If you choose not to give your kid a portable digital device, you are far from alone. A Piedmont mom I know held strong against getting her seventh-grade daughter a phone or watch. She noted with pride that her daughter had become resourceful about finding the right adult to speak to when she needed assistance. “I told her to find a mom or a nanny, or in the center of town, to talk to someone working at Mulberry’s or a police officer.” Now, she says, her daughter is glad she doesn’t have a device because “I’m not brought into the crazy drama that is happening” among friends on group texts. “I used to think I would be uncool and missing out, but this year, I don’t care.” Amanda Straub is a co-founder of Piedmont Unplugged ADVERTISE IN THE POST

articles.text: Finance Director Kiran Bawa reported to the City Council that the city had ended the year approximately $2.3 million above initial budget projections. Piedmont generated $1.5 million in additional revenue, while expenditures came in $837,000 below budget expectations. On the recommendation of Bawa and the Budget Advisory Committee, the City Council unanimously voted to transfer $1.7 million to the city’s Facilities Capital Fund and $200,000 to the Facilities Maintenance Fund. The Facilities Capital Fund and Maintenance Fund manage the city’s facility renovations, major capital improvements, and preventative maintenance. This year, the Capital Fund spent $5.1 million on projects such as the community pool, the finalization of the police dispatch center, the Linda Beach Tot Lot, the Piedmont Park pathway, and the storm drains. Council member Jennifer Long asked Bawa how they arrived at these numbers and why they prioritized these funds. Bawa explained that they look at how the General Fund ended the fiscal year and determine how much money they could use to help other areas. They then analyze the five- to 10-year outlook of their internal funds to determine which of them need additional help from the General Fund. They determined these funds needed to be prioritized because they lack regular revenue sources, especially for the Capital Fund. The city’s transfer tax generated $5.9 million, exceeding budget projections by 40%. This year, the city generated the thirdmost transfer tax revenue since the pandemic years of 2020 and 2021. In 2026, 135 homes were sold, which is 9% more than the 124 homes sold in the prior year. The average sales price was $3.36 million, approx. 18% higher than the prior year’s $2.85 million. Although these numbers sound great, Bawa warned council members about the volatility of this income. Bawa showed the council a graph of the year-over-year percentage change of property taxes and transfer taxes. The graph showed a stable line for property taxes, while transfer taxes spiked significantly. It showed years like 2015-2016 where the transfer tax revenue decreased by 20%, and only a few years later, in 2020, the chart spiked to a 75% increase in transfer tax revenue. Bawa emphasized that the city exercises caution in relying on these revenues to support ongoing operating expenses because of the housing market’s volatility. “Our real estate transfer tax came in $1.7 million over budget. Our overall revenues are $1.5 million over budget, so all other revenues came in $200,000 less than budget. The volatility is that if the transfer tax dives the other direction, it can hurt us more than minus $200,000,” said Bawa. Following these transfers, the General Fund will retain $7.0 million, or 18% of operating expenditures, maintaining the city’s historical reserve practice. The results presented at the meeting are still preliminary and unaudited. They remain subject to adjustments once auditing is complete.
articles.title: Piedmont’s year-end audit comes in $2.3 million above budget projections

articles.text: The holiday spirit is coming to Montclair Village as the neighborhood celebrates its 24th Annual Holiday Stroll on Thursday, December 10, from 4:30 to 8 p.m. Presented by the Montclair Village Association, this free, family-friendly celebration invites Oakland residents and visitors to experience the magic of the season with an evening of live entertainment, festive activities, holiday shopping, food and drinks, and plenty of community cheer. Families can make special holiday memories with professional Winter Wonderland photos with Santa, taken by Leah Marie Studio ($35). A dedicated family zone will keep younger visitors entertained with glow-in-the-dark face painting by Lily’s Arte, storytime led by the Montclair Oakland Public Library, and holiday crafts hosted by St. John’s Episcopal Church, Montclair Presbyterian Church, and Red Oak Realty team members Marissa Verson Harrison and Ilan Penson. The Oakland Fire Department’s parade rig will host the Random Acts Toy Drive with a toy donation bin located at Montclair Toyhouse. Visitors can also support the Alameda County Community Food Bank at its event booth. The Hospitality Hut will feature a full bar serving festive libations and hot cocoa. Proceeds from the Hospitality Hut will benefit future arts and cultural programming and beautification projects in the district. Holiday retail pop-up vendors will offer additional opportunities to discover artisan-made gifts and seasonal finds. “The Holiday Stroll is a wonderful opportunity to bring our community together, celebrate the season, and shine a spotlight on the unique businesses that make Montclair Village such a special neighborhood,” said Daniel Swafford, executive director of the Montclair Village Association. Admission and entertainment are free. Convenient parking is available at the Montclair Garage, located at 6235 LaSalle Avenue in Oakland. More information on musical performances, special promotions, giveaways, sweets & treats that over 40 village businesses will offer is available online at www.montclairvillage. com/holiday-stroll.
articles.title: Montclair Village hosts 24th annual Holiday Stroll on Dec. 10

articles.text: As winter temperatures and rains befall the Bay Area, Wildwood third grade Girl Scouts of Troop 32125 are teaming up with Girl Scouts of Northern California and One Warm Coat to share warmth. Troop 32125 is asking area residents to look through their closets for a clean coat or jacket in good condition that’s ready for a new home. Donations make an immediate impact in the local community by providing those in need with a tangible gift, protection from the elements. Donations of coats and jackets are being accepted through November 30. “It’s part of our Girl Scout oath to help others. We are happy to help less fortunate people who don’t have warm coats for the winter,” said Girl Scout Siena Paley. The troop is hoping to collect at least 50 coats, which will be donated to Community Action Alliance, an Oakland nonprofit that provides housing and economic support in partnership with One Warm Coat. Last year, more than 4,000 individuals, organizations and companies across the country worked with One Warm Coat to collect nearly 500,000 coats, which were distributed to children and adults in need across the United States. “This project brings me joy. I really like helping less fortunate people find coats. Make sure to donate a coat!” said Girl Scout Hayden Driskill. Coats can be dropped off outside the front doors of Wildwood Elementary or on the porches of 1042 Annerley Road or 154 Wildwood Gardens. Coats are needed in all sizes, but especially men’s coats and jackets. About One Warm Coat Founded in 1992 by one woman with one coat to give, One Warm Coat is a national nonprofit organization that originated with one simple act of kindness. With a deep-seated belief in the power of collective action, One Warm Coat engages and supports thousands of volunteers each year to collect coats, sharing warmth with half a million people in need in communities nationwide. Over the past 34 years, One Warm Coat has distributed nearly 9 million coats through a network of 1,500 local nonprofit partners, keeping more than 22 million pounds of textiles out of landfills. Visit onewarmcoat.org today to learn how individuals and organizations can engage with One Warm Coat’s mission to share warmth, not waste. Girl Scout Troop 32125 crafted this donation box to accept winter coats for those in need. Donations can be made in front of Wildwood School or on the porches of 1042 Annerley Road and 154 Wildwood Gardens.

articles.text: Piedmont Community Church (PCC) will host two performances of its 16th annual Christmas Concert performed by a full orchestra and choir on Saturday, December 5, and Sunday, December 6, both at 7:30 p.m. The music runs about an hour and each of the identical shows are followed by festive receptions with a smorgasbord of food and wine. PCC Composer & Conductor Stephen Main and former PCC President Patricia Leicher launched the annual Christmas Concert at PCC in 2011 as a way to bring the sound of a full orchestra to the church. This year the Christmas Concerts will have 34 orchestral players and 44 choir singers, performing non-commercial Christmas music. The program starts and finishes with carols at the beginning and the end that the whole audience sings along to. “This is huge. This is not just a little church sing-along with some carols and somebody at the piano. This is a full orchestra singing, and there’s nothing like it, and people really boom out. It’s lots of fun,” said Main. Main is a bit of a Christmas historian, and he uses his research on the evolution of the holiday to present a concert curated to the theme, this year’s is Joy and Good Cheer, An Overture to Christmas. “Before Neiman Marcus and all the other interests out there get their hooks into everybody and define the holiday for you, we get to define it, hopefully in a good way for people,” said Main. Main explained Christmas has evolved a lot in the last 1,000 years from a very minor holiday that was no more important than Piedmont Community Church hosts two showings of their 16th annual Christmas Concert on December 5 and 6. “Michaelmas,” a feast day for St. Michael that started in the 4th century. Main’s studies also uncovered an ancient version of caroling that was more like trickor-treating. Hard-working folk would mass together as carolers to sing at the residence of the affluent and remain until the gentry shared their food and wine. Main finds some songs for the concert from ancient texts and ancient tunes that people don’t know. Aside from the singalongs at the start and the end, the body of the program is a top-notch musical experience for an adult audience. Laura Taylor, PCC’s Director of Communications, will also be singing in the concert. “As a member of the choir I must say Steve has an incredibly high caliber set of standards. He composes music, he rewrites hymns, he’s amazing. What Steve does is truly magical,” said Taylor. Having the Christmas event in the first week of December not only gives Main and PCC the chance to set the tone of the holiday season, but it also lets them book the best talent around. These same performers are fully booked up in high-priced concerts later in the month. While power was lost to tens of thousands of Bay Area residents, 40 Piedmont Post newspaper carriers braved the storm to deliver dry papers to subscribers all over town. Rain in the Grand Lake area reached 1.92 inches by mid-afternoon last Wednesday, making for a wet paper delivery day. Slogging up the hills with ponchos and umbrellas, more than 1,100 subscribers, apologies to the exceptions, received their weekly rag as did hundreds of non-subscribing residents as part of the “all-city” delivery. “When it was raining on Wednesday, I thought delivering papers would be horrible, but it wasn’t that bad. It was like the universe said ‘it is time to deliver papers, why don’t you slow down this rain,” said Zoe Selor, a sixth grade paper carrier. November’s delivery schedule has had its conflicts for paper carriers: November 11 was Veterans Day, November 18 brought the big rain and this delivery November 25 finds many schedule conflicts with carriers out of town for Thanksgiving. This reporter, tasked with managing the delivery carriers over the last year, took to the streets on Friday, November 20 to deliver some papers on Crocker, Wildwood and Lincoln Avenues as well. The distance between houses, and the sometimes unorthodox numbering of Piedmont homes, drove home an appreciation for what Piedmont’s army of newspaper delivery kids accomplishes every week. The Piedmont Post celebrated 28 years of being in print in October. When the paper was founded on Tuesday, October 20, 1998, Publisher Gray Cathrall started with a delivery team of six. The first six weekly editions of the Post, at 12 pages apiece, went to every house in the city. “After that we delivered to subscribers only, around 400 houses, and residents understood you had to subscribe,” said Cathrall. Cathrall remembers the team of delivery kids steadily rising over time to around 30 in the 2000s. This tradition is still alive, and has provided first jobs for hundreds of Piedmont kids. “In our increasingly digital world, where so much of our information is delivered and consumed on screens, there is something refreshing about having our local news delivered in print by the wonderful children of Piedmont,” said subscriber Evren Essner. Selor, in her second year of work for the paper, has learned lessons of responsibility and hard work. “The paper route taught me that even if I don’t want to deliver papers, I don’t have a choice because people are counting on me. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team wrapped up its season in a solid way at the 2026 Division 2 North Coast Section Individual Tournament on Monday and Tuesday, November 16-17 at the La Cantera Racquet Club in Santa Rosa. In the singles bracket, sophomore Ella Ruthven placed fourth overall, while seniors Emma Chan and Faith Chin also placed fourth in the doubles ladder. “It was a wonderful season with a lot of great tennis, a plethora of coaches, an abundance of laughter and good times for all. We finished 13-7 and made it into the NCS Division 1 team tournament,” coach Jim Landes said. “We played so many exciting matches, I can’t remember a year with so many 4-3 results. The girls all competed well and improved so much. More importantly, they had a lot of fun along the way,” assistant coach Corey Reich added. For Ruthven, she opened the tournament with a 6-2, 6-0 win over Samyuktha Rangarajan of Quarry Lane. In the quarterfinals, Ruthven handily defeated Terra Linda’s Kylie Lee in straight sets, 6-1, 6-0. The following day, Ruthven fell to Leila Rouda of Lick Wilmerding 6-2, 7-6 (7-4). Rouda went on to win this year’s singles title. Ruthven faced Lick Wilmerding’s Leena Kambara in the third-place final and similarly lost in a heated second-set tiebreaker, 6-3, 7-6 (9-7). articles.text: Girls’ Volleyball won Piedmont High’s first-ever North Coast Section title this fall. Another fall season has come and gone for Piedmont High. Here is taking a look at some of the key highlights from the 2026 fall season. Girls Volleyball wins first NCS title in school history The girls’ volleyball team had a historic season this fall, winning the school’s first-ever North Coast Section title on November 7. In the Division 3 bracket, PHS’ No. 3 ranked team beat No. 5 San Domenico in a comeback five-set match by scores of 25-18, 23-25, 22-25, 25-11, 15-7. To get there, they beat No. 14 San Leandro 3-0 in the opening round on October 27, swept No. 11 Clayton Valley 3-0 on October 31, and upset No. 2 Justin-Siena 3-1 on November 4. Reaching the D3 bracket was a full division jump from 2025 after playing in D4 as the No. 8 seed, while 2027 is shaping up to be another strong campaign. Potentially returning to the group Ella Ruthven won this year’s Western Alameda County Conference singles title. Boys’ Water Polo played their first match at the Piedmont Pool since 2019 due to renovations. Staff Photos next year includes Maika Ting, Olivia Stevens, Mia Bechtel, Izara Dando, Sofia Meyer, Lucia Dorsey, Carina Vora, Charlotte Bailey, Hazel Schaeffer, Devon Porter, Emilia Angulo, Sofie Bechtel, and Sarina Hill. Ella Ruthven wins WACC singles title Ella Ruthven put together a strong campaign as a sophomore in 2026, winning the Western Alameda County Conference singles title on November 7. As the No. 1 seed, she defeated No. 2 seed Ellena Kau of Bishop O’Dowd in three sets after dropping the first in a 2-6, 6-1, 6-4 victory. Ruthven opened the tournament with a 6-0, 6-1 win over Berkeley Cambria Frozena, shutout Castro Valley’s Claire Liu 6-0, 6-0 in the quarterfinals, and also swept her Piedmont teammate Maddy Huynh 6-0, 6-0 in the semifinals. Her singles title marked the school’s first since Tanya Kononova did so as a junior in 2022. Boys’ Water Polo at Piedmont Pool & berth in D1 NCS One of the hallmark moments of the fall didn’t have to with accolades. On September 3, Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team played its first match at the Piedmont Pool since 2019 after renovations of the site elapsed over six years. As for the Highlanders’ results, this year’s team received a berth in the Division 1 NCS bracket for the first time as the No. 16 seed. PHS lost to No. 1 Northgate 15-6 on November 5. Despite the loss, the Highlanders look ahead to 2027 with a lot of optimism. Henry Stein and Rylan Patty will lead the charge as seniors, while they will be accompanied by current sophomores like Dylan Jerez, Ben Kappes and Wilson Walker.

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team returns for the start of their regular season on November 28 against Marin Academy. Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team gets their season started on Saturday, November 28 when hosting Marin Academy at Binks Rawlings Gym. The Highlanders do so with a cast that mixes experienced starters with incoming sophomores after finishing in last year’s D2 North Coast Section quarterfinals with the No. 4 seed and a 19-9 overall record. Back in the fold is Beach Lorin for his third-year as a varsity player as a senior. He headlines the group alongside starting guard Lucian Fang-Ring, while fellow senior Will Hinman is also poised for big minutes. Spencer thinks Lorin has improved as a defender and physical presence. He finished last season second on the team in scoring behind Dillon Casey, who now plays at Occidental College. “Beach was a unanimous All-League first-team selection last year, which is a pretty big honor. He’s a tremendous scorer and an offensive juggernaut. He’s actually gotten really good defensively and has become one of our best defenders. He’s really improved in rebounding, and is our biggest inside presence. We made it a point that he goes after every rebound on the defensive side,” coach Ben Spencer said. As for Fang-Ring, Spencer praised his accurate shooting after finishing last season strongly. “This will be his third year as a starter, he’s a tough kid. He’s a captain, an unbelievable leader, and a hard worker. He got off to a slow start last year and was cold in the first 10 games, but then picked it up late in the year. That’s carried over into this year and has been shooting the lights out this whole preseason and offseason,” Spencer said. articles.text: On Sunday, November 8, junior rowing crews from around the Bay Area gathered in Foster City for the annual Head of the Lagoon regatta. Nearly two dozen Piedmont rowers turned in strong performances, earning several top-three finishes for their Oakland Strokes rowing teams. A staple of Northern California’s autumn rowing calendar, the Head of the Lagoon is held each November as the final major head race of the fall season. The two-day regatta typically draws between 300 and 500 boat entries across all classes, from single sculls to coxed eights. The event is a traditional “head race,” a time-trial format in which boats launch one at a time at rolling intervals of 10 to 20 seconds. Winners are decided by total elapsed time rather than by a head-to-head sprint to the finish line. The 5-kilometer (roughly 3.1-mile) course starts at the southern tip of the lagoon and winds along a path shaped like the numeral “2.” Crews pass beneath three bridges and along the Central Lake boardwalk before finishing near the Port O’ Call Shopping Center. The two-day Head of the Lagoon regatta featured Masters, Open, Jr1x single-scullers and college racing on Saturday, November 7 and junior racing on Sunday. Oakland Strokes entered 30 crews at the Head of the Lagoon on Sunday, winning 11 podium finishes (three gold, four silver, and four bronze). “We’re proud of how the team raced together in our last fall regatta,” said Dana Hooper, Executive Director of the Oakland Strokes. “What stands out is how much these athletes care about each other. That will carry them through a hard winter of training and into the spring season.” Piedmont podium finishes In the Women’s Junior 8+, Amelia Callaway (seat 2) and Paige Young (bow seat) rowed to a second-place finish out of five crews, with a time of 19:15.4. Sophia Brenner, rowing in seat 6, helped her crew take third of five at 19:32.3. The junior Men’s crews also made their mark. In the Men’s Junior Youth 8+, the Strokes scored second and third. Connor Cross, rowing in seat 6 of the Burke III boat, helped his team earn second place with a time of 16:20.1. Diego Branneria, in seat 7 of the N Hudson boat, helped his crew to third place at 16:31.3. In the Men’s Junior 2V 8+, Mattias Rael, in seat 5 of the Shepherd boat (308), took third with a time of 17:59.0. About Oakland Strokes Founded in 1974 by Olympic rower and Cal sculler Ed Lickiss, the Oakland Strokes Rowing Club is one of the nation’s premier nonprofit youth rowing programs. With daily afternoon practice in the East Bay’s Oakland Estuary, the club serves student-athletes in grades 6 through 12. Over its 52-year history, the program has grown into a competitive powerhouse, capturing 24 USRowing National Championships. Beyond athletic excellence, the club emphasizes leadership, teamwork, and fellowship. Its rowers regularly go on to top collegiate programs across the country, including Ivy League schools and NCAA Division I teams. articles.text: A new exhibition at the de Young museum in San Francisco brings together Pueblo pottery traditions and classic cars through two customized vehicles by Santa Clara Pueblo artist Rose B. Simpson. The exhibition features Maria, a 1985 Chevrolet El Camino that Simpson refurbished in 2014 and decorated with a black-on-black Tewa pottery motif, and Bosque, a 1964 Buick Riviera painted in vibrant multicolored designs. The latter marks the debut of Simpson’s second customized car, created 10 years after Maria. Simpson named the first car in honor of Maria Martinez, a renowned San Ildefonso Pueblo potter (1887-1980) who helped popularize the distinctive blackon-black pottery style. articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre is presenting Liberation, a play by Bess Wohl that examines the women’s liberation movement of the 1970s, now through November 29. The play received the 2026 Pulitzer Prize for Drama and Tony Award for Best Play following its Broadway run. Set in 1970s Ohio, the play follows Lizzie, who brings together a group of women in a recreation center basement to discuss their lives and work toward social change. Decades later, Lizzie’s daughter explores her mother’s history, revisiting the group’s discussions and examining questions about women’s freedom and equality. The production moves between the two generations, exploring the relationship between the feminist movement’s original goals and the questions that remain unresolved. “Berkeley has a very special relationship to the history of the women’s movement, having fostered and produced many champions of women’s rights who laid the foundations of the movement and continue to push us forward today,” White said in a press release. “Liberation was a labor of love and resistance, and I cannot wait for audiences to meet these unforgettable characters.” The cast includes Katie Lowes as Lizzie, Felicia Curry as Celeste, Britt Faulkner as Dora, Irene Sofia Lucio as Isidora, Gunnar Manchester as Bill, Mary Gordon Murray as Margie, Veronica Otim as Joanna and Evelyn Spahr as Susan. articles.text: An intimate documentary follows a group of exiles determined to tell their country the truth. What does a citizen owe to their country? And what if that country is Russia? Such is the moral dilemma afflicting the characters of My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile, Julia Loktev’s sequel to her acclaimed 2024 documentary about the unraveling of Russia’s last independent television channel, Dozhd (or TV Rain), in the wake of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The first installment chronicles the channel’s final days in Moscow in March of 2022, and Part II follows its journalists into exile. Loktev’s protagonists, almost all women, f led as Russia imposed censorship laws that made their already dangerous jobs punishable by up to 15 years in prison. Within days of Dozhd’s disbandment, sometimes hours, they scooped up their laptops, pets, children, and underwear and flew wherever they could without a new visa—Istanbul, Tbilisi, Prague, Tel Aviv. They resisted Russian President Vladimir Putin and his government, yet wherever they go, they remain citizens of a country that is invading and killing its neighbors and are held responsible for the war it wages in their name. “You feel like it’s 1941 and you’re simultaneously the German and the Jew,” says journalist Anna Nemzer, as she reloads her vape cartridge. Loktev’s subjects are buffeted by cognitive dissonance and must constantly explain themselves— to their Georgian and Latvian hosts, who urge them to “tell Putin to stop the war”; to their Ukrainian sources, who resent the very language that they speak; to their Russian parents who tell them to stop writing anti-government “bullshit” and come home; and even to themselves, wondering what they could have done differently to stop their country’s slide into fascism, and whether their work matters when Russian missiles continue to rain down on Ukraine. Loktev, who shot the film herself on an iPhone, gives these questions room. At six hours, this film is even longer than its predecessor—a bold choice—but the sheer accumulation of ordinary moments makes this exploration of exile intimate and compelling. For viewers willing to grapple with existential dilemmas and lucky enough to live near an arthouse cinema, the movie’s length may be a boon. After all, its central questions are ones that take a lifetime to sort out. Perhaps no one takes up these questions more bluntly than Elena Kostyuchenko of the recently shuttered Novaya Gazeta, where, during her tenure, four of her colleagues were murdered. “All of us … spent many years, thoroughly, in great detail, in very good, wellwritten articles describing the coming of fascism in Russia,” she says. “Well, there you fucking go. So we wrote all those articles.” Elsewhere, she is just as unsparing about the failure to stop Putin from turning Russia into what it is today: “We didn’t want to sacrifice our comfort.” Nataliya Gumenyuk, a prominent Ukrainian journalist and war correspondent who is married to a longtime former Dozhd journalist. “We live in our own country and continue to do our work.” Among the movie’s most striking images is that of Ukrainians dancing in a square in Kharkiv, where entire blocks are flattened by air strikes, the sound of Ukrainian folk songs mixing with the howling of the air raid sirens. Nataliya’s Russian husband, Peter, resolved his moral dilemma by joining the Ukrainian army and now records his F**k the War! podcast between missions. From its new home in the Netherlands, the “optimistic channel,” as Dozhd was once known, still reaches 13 million as of 2023, according to Dozhd. Because coverage of the war not aligning with Kremlin narratives has been all but silenced, most watch through VPNs and proxies. For journalists, reporting on Russia’s war means living the Russian reality. This makes integration into their new countries nearly impossible; they are neither here nor there. But going home is not an option. Ratnikova, for one, was sentenced to seven-and-a-half years in prison in absentia by a Moscow court. Loktev records her hearing over a video call, where “witnesses” explain how the “false information” about the war “confused” them. This is how Russian justice works. A lesya Ma rok hovskaya expresses similar unease as she recalls watching someone get beaten at a protest. “My job is to film,” she says. “You don’t rush in to defend the person. You film them, because, well, that’s your job.” Despite those doubts, the journalists keep doing journalism. They provide truthful coverage of the war to Russian-speaking audiences through YouTube channels, podcasts, and eventually live broadcasts from Riga, Latvia, where Dozhd secured a broadcasting license. But they are walking on eggshells. A series of on-air missteps that led to questions about the station’s allegiances ultimately cost Dozhd its initial broadcasting license, forcing it to relocate to the Netherlands, where it operates today. The hope of finding safety outside Russia does not last long. Alesya and her best friend Irina Dolinina, investigative journalists with IStories (or Important Stories), now based in Prague, receive oddly specific anonymous threats. The senders know their passport numbers, flight reservations, even about Alesya’s “snorting” bulldog. New friends are not always who they say they are: A supposed human rights lawyer Irina befriends previously worked for Moscow police. Alesya’s father, meanwhile, doesn’t understand why his daughter left. The war is in Ukraine, he says, not Russia. But for most of these women, war is everywhere. From a temporary shelter in a Swiss village, where cathedral bells mark the hours of another peaceful day, Kostyuchenko recounts the symptoms of what she believes was a deliberate poisoning in Munich in October 2022: foul sweat, disorientation, nausea, swollen extremities. Months before, reporting from the Ukrainian city of Mykolaiv, Kostyuchenko had visited a morgue overflowing with victims of Russian shelling, which she wrote about with brutal clarity. “In the fridge, the bodies are stacked in layers. Two girls lie on top of each other. They’re sisters. The older one is 17—in the heap of bodies, all I can see is her hand, long thin fingers with a neat pink manicure. The younger is 3—she lies on top of her sister. … Her body is dotted with red shrapnel wounds. The girl looks alive.” Despite atrocities that should have stopped the world in its tracks, life goes on, and Loktev’s film captures that well. Kostyuchenko loves, and loves deeply. Her partner is Yana Kuchina, a Moscow book editor turned disability-rights advocate who followed Kostyuchenko into exile. A newcomer to Loktev’s saga, Yana delivers some of the film’s most chilling insights into how Russia treats its own. Her cerebral palsy, she says, is considered an “intellectual inadequacy” in the eyes of the authorities, barring her from getting a driver’s license, becoming a doctor, or adopting a child. Besides Yana, Kostyuchenko loves her mother—whose birthday she is missing for the first time—and her country. Her life there, she felt, was real. “I worked at the best newspaper on Earth. … All around me was my country, which I … value and love still.” Her love is definitely not blind, but for Ukrainians, whose country Russia is destroying, it may be difficult to comprehend, much less forgive. Unlike Elena and Yana, former Dozhd reporter Ksenia (Ksyusha) Mironova walks the road of exile alone, a melancholy kaleidoscope of taxi rides, dark staircases, and endless rented rooms; her fiancé, the journalist Ivan Safronov, is still being held in a Moscow prison on fabricated charges of high treason. Ksyusha returns to Russia for his sentencing, a trip Loktev also documents. Ivan gets 22 years. In the midst of so much loss, there are brief moments of tenderness. In a rented apartment abroad, Ksyusha and her Dozhd friends sing along to a Russian song: “When you return … I hope we recognize each other … and I am not your wife and not even your girlfriend.” It is probably the most Russian scene in the entire movie—elegiac, haunting, yet oddly hopeful. Ksyusha is neither a victim nor a tragic heroine; behind her soft, girlish looks is a rod of steel. No longer with Dozhd, she moves from country to country, taking whatever freelance jobs she can find to keep herself afloat and working as an independent journalist covering political prisoners, their families, and the lives of Russians in exile. In 2025, we see her in the United States reporting on President Donald Trump’s second inauguration. “It’s really strange I’m now in America and the same things are happening here,” she says. She now works with Nemzer to archive independent journalism, including to preserve two decades of coverage in Russia against the Kremlin’s attempts to erase it. Sonya Groysman, another Dozhd journalist, finds ingenious ways to report on Russia from exile, directing anonymous camera operators, including wedding videographers. One of her reports features Sasha Skochilenko, an artist who was sentenced to seven years in prison for replacing price tags in a St. Petersburg supermarket with anti-war messages. The camera zooms in on a black-andwhite tag above the coffee cans reading “Russia’s Army bombed Mariupol art school where 400 people hid from shelling.” It’s yet another reminder that in Russia, the price of truth is your freedom. Or your life. A sizable part of the documentary is devoted to the 2024 death of opposition leader Alexey Navalny. Dozhd, broadcasting from Amsterdam, ran videos of him from the day before his death, where he looks energetic and fairly healthy. In their coverage, the presenters called his death in prison what many in Russia knew but were afraid to say: a killing. Navalny went to prison to change people’s minds, says tearful Valeria Ratnikova, a Dozhd news anchor, between the airings of her show. He was a beacon for many. Now, all she sees is “total blackness ahead.” The only characters spared this Dostoyevskian moral anguish are, unsurprisingly, Ukrainian. “We don’t have the energy and time to worry and panic,” says For now, Ratnikova has a visa, a job, a place to stay. That could change overnight. Political exile is not war, but that’s a low bar for young men and women who could have lived a relatively normal life. By reporting independently, first in an increasingly authoritarian state, then from exile, often at considerable risk to themselves, they have given more to their country than its perpetually silent majority. One of Ratnikova’s colleagues likens their mission to Sisyphus pushing his stone uphill: not as punishment, but by choice. They keep at it, hoping their work might still change minds in a country that seems irretrievably lost. Loktev’s immersion in their lives leaves us with hope for them, if not for Russia’s future. Anastasia Edel is a Russian-born American writer and social historian. She is the author of Russia: Putin’s Playground, a concise guide to Russian history, politics, and culture. pages.text: 18 Wednesday, November 25, 2026 RECENT RELEASE By Anastasia Edel What does a citizen owe to their country? And what if that country is Russia? Such is the moral dilemma afflicting the characters of My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile, Julia Loktev’s sequel to her acclaimed 2024 documentary about the unraveling of Russia’s last independent television channel, Dozhd (or TV Rain), in the wake of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The first installment chronicles the channel’s final days in Moscow in March of 2022, and Part II follows its journalists into exile. Loktev’s protagonists, almost all women, f led as Russia imposed censorship laws that made their already dangerous jobs punishable by up to 15 years in prison. Within days of Dozhd’s disbandment, sometimes hours, they scooped up their laptops, pets, children, and underwear and flew wherever they could without a new visa—Istanbul, Tbilisi, Prague, Tel Aviv. They resisted Russian President Vladimir Putin and his government, yet wherever they go, they remain citizens of a country that is invading and killing its neighbors and are held responsible for the war it wages in their name. “You feel like it’s 1941 and you’re simultaneously the German and the Jew,” says journalist Anna Nemzer, as she reloads her vape cartridge. Loktev’s subjects are buffeted by cognitive dissonance and must constantly explain themselves— to their Georgian and Latvian hosts, who urge them to “tell Putin to stop the war”; to their Ukrainian sources, who resent the very language that they speak; to their Russian parents who tell them to stop writing anti-government “bullshit” and come home; and even to themselves, wondering what they could have done differently to stop their country’s slide into fascism, and whether their work matters when Russian missiles continue to rain down on Ukraine. Loktev, who shot the film herself on an iPhone, gives these questions room. At six hours, this film is even longer than its predecessor—a bold choice—but the sheer accumulation of ordinary moments makes this exploration of exile intimate and compelling. For viewers willing to grapple with existential dilemmas and lucky enough to live near an arthouse cinema, the movie’s length may be a boon. After all, its central questions are ones that take a lifetime to sort out. Perhaps no one takes up these questions more bluntly than Elena Kostyuchenko of the recently shuttered Novaya Gazeta, where, during her tenure, four of her colleagues were murdered. “All of us … spent many years, thoroughly, in great detail, in very good, wellwritten articles describing the coming of fascism in Russia,” she says. “Well, there you fucking go. So we wrote all those articles.” Elsewhere, she is just as unsparing about the failure to stop Putin from turning Russia into what it is today: “We didn’t want to sacrifice our comfort.” Nataliya Gumenyuk, a prominent Ukrainian journalist and war correspondent who is married to a longtime former Dozhd journalist. “We live in our own country and continue to do our work.” Among the movie’s most striking images is that of Ukrainians dancing in a square in Kharkiv, where entire blocks are flattened by air strikes, the sound of Ukrainian folk songs mixing with the howling of the air raid sirens. Nataliya’s Russian husband, Peter, resolved his moral dilemma by joining the Ukrainian army and now records his F**k the War! podcast between missions. From its new home in the Netherlands, the “optimistic channel,” as Dozhd was once known, still reaches 13 million as of 2023, according to Dozhd. Because coverage of the war not aligning with Kremlin narratives has been all but silenced, most watch through VPNs and proxies. For journalists, reporting on Russia’s war means living the Russian reality. This makes integration into their new countries nearly impossible; they are neither here nor there. But going home is not an option. Ratnikova, for one, was sentenced to seven-and-a-half years in prison in absentia by a Moscow court. Loktev records her hearing over a video call, where “witnesses” explain how the “false information” about the war “confused” them. This is how Russian justice works. The journalists who left Russia—but can’t escape it An intimate documentary follows a group of exiles determined to tell their country the truth. A lesya Ma rok hovskaya expresses similar unease as she recalls watching someone get beaten at a protest. “My job is to film,” she says. “You don’t rush in to defend the person. You film them, because, well, that’s your job.” Despite those doubts, the journalists keep doing journalism. They provide truthful coverage of the war to Russian-speaking audiences through YouTube channels, podcasts, and eventually live broadcasts from Riga, Latvia, where Dozhd secured a broadcasting license. But they are walking on eggshells. A series of on-air missteps that led to questions about the station’s allegiances ultimately cost Dozhd its initial broadcasting license, forcing it to relocate to the Netherlands, where it operates today. The hope of finding safety outside Russia does not last long. Alesya and her best friend Irina Dolinina, investigative journalists with IStories (or Important Stories), now based in Prague, receive oddly specific anonymous threats. The senders know their passport numbers, flight reservations, even about Alesya’s “snorting” bulldog. New friends are not always who they say they are: A supposed human rights lawyer Irina befriends previously worked for Moscow police. Alesya’s father, meanwhile, doesn’t understand why his daughter left. The war is in Ukraine, he says, not Russia. But for most of these women, war is everywhere. From a temporary shelter in a Swiss village, where cathedral bells mark the hours of another peaceful day, Kostyuchenko recounts the symptoms of what she believes was a deliberate poisoning in Munich in October 2022: foul sweat, disorientation, nausea, swollen extremities. Months before, reporting from the Ukrainian city of Mykolaiv, Kostyuchenko had visited a morgue overflowing with victims of Russian shelling, which she wrote about with brutal clarity. “In the fridge, the bodies are stacked in layers. Two girls lie on top of each other. They’re sisters. The older one is 17—in the heap of bodies, all I can see is her hand, long thin fingers with a neat pink manicure. The younger is 3—she lies on top of her sister. … Her body is dotted with red shrapnel wounds. The girl looks alive.” Despite atrocities that should have stopped the world in its tracks, life goes on, and Loktev’s film captures that well. Kostyuchenko loves, and loves deeply. Her partner is Yana Kuchina, a Moscow book editor turned disability-rights advocate who followed Kostyuchenko into exile. A newcomer to Loktev’s saga, Yana delivers some of the film’s most chilling insights into how Russia treats its own. Her cerebral palsy, she says, is considered an “intellectual inadequacy” in the eyes of the authorities, barring her from getting a driver’s license, becoming a doctor, or adopting a child. Besides Yana, Kostyuchenko loves her mother—whose birthday she is missing for the first time—and her country. Her life there, she felt, was real. “I worked at the best newspaper on Earth. … All around me was my country, which I … value and love still.” Her love is definitely not blind, but for Ukrainians, whose country Russia is destroying, it may be difficult to comprehend, much less forgive. Unlike Elena and Yana, former Dozhd reporter Ksenia (Ksyusha) Mironova walks the road of exile alone, a melancholy kaleidoscope of taxi rides, dark staircases, and endless rented rooms; her fiancé, the journalist Ivan Safronov, is still being held in a Moscow prison on fabricated charges of high treason. Ksyusha returns to Russia for his sentencing, a trip Loktev also documents. Ivan gets 22 years. In the midst of so much loss, there are brief moments of tenderness. In a rented apartment abroad, Ksyusha and her Dozhd friends sing along to a Russian song: “When you return … I hope we recognize each other … and I am not your wife and not even your girlfriend.” It is probably the most Russian scene in the entire movie—elegiac, haunting, yet oddly hopeful. Ksyusha is neither a victim nor a tragic heroine; behind her soft, girlish looks is a rod of steel. No longer with Dozhd, she moves from country to country, taking whatever freelance jobs she can find to keep herself afloat and working as an independent journalist covering political prisoners, their families, and the lives of Russians in exile. In 2025, we see her in the United States reporting on President Donald Trump’s second inauguration. “It’s really strange I’m now in America and the same things are happening here,” she says. She now works with Nemzer to archive independent journalism, including to preserve two decades of coverage in Russia against the Kremlin’s attempts to erase it. Sonya Groysman, another Dozhd journalist, finds ingenious ways to report on Russia from exile, directing anonymous camera operators, including wedding videographers. One of her reports features Sasha Skochilenko, an artist who was sentenced to seven years in prison for replacing price tags in a St. Petersburg supermarket with anti-war messages. The camera zooms in on a black-andwhite tag above the coffee cans reading “Russia’s Army bombed Mariupol art school where 400 people hid from shelling.” It’s yet another reminder that in Russia, the price of truth is your freedom. Or your life. A sizable part of the documentary is devoted to the 2024 death of opposition leader Alexey Navalny. Dozhd, broadcasting from Amsterdam, ran videos of him from the day before his death, where he looks energetic and fairly healthy. In their coverage, the presenters called his death in prison what many in Russia knew but were afraid to say: a killing. Navalny went to prison to change people’s minds, says tearful Valeria Ratnikova, a Dozhd news anchor, between the airings of her show. He was a beacon for many. Now, all she sees is “total blackness ahead.” The only characters spared this Dostoyevskian moral anguish are, unsurprisingly, Ukrainian. “We don’t have the energy and time to worry and panic,” says For now, Ratnikova has a visa, a job, a place to stay. That could change overnight. Political exile is not war, but that’s a low bar for young men and women who could have lived a relatively normal life. By reporting independently, first in an increasingly authoritarian state, then from exile, often at considerable risk to themselves, they have given more to their country than its perpetually silent majority. One of Ratnikova’s colleagues likens their mission to Sisyphus pushing his stone uphill: not as punishment, but by choice. They keep at it, hoping their work might still change minds in a country that seems irretrievably lost. Loktev’s immersion in their lives leaves us with hope for them, if not for Russia’s future. His 12-day adventure provided Michael with a new type of inspiration: totally new architectural silhouettes, blasts of vivid color, and a sea of friendly faces. In the end, The Land of the Rising Sun provided a sledgehammer of stimulus that led to the creation of new work. This year’s exhibit included 28 new paintings of Japan, Rome, and Paris. This exhibit will close after open gallery hours on Sunday, November 29, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Friday, December 4, 7:00 p.m. Lights Out Piano Quartet Concert Every musical journey has its own many characters: moments of discovery and reflection, passages of beauty and elegance, and of course, drama and intensity. This quartet, led by pianist Amy Zanrosso, and including violinist Cuna Kim, violist Mitso Floor, and cellist Kyle Stachnik, invites you to enjoy The Scenic Route: A Piano Quartet Journey by travelling with them into three distinctive musical worlds, beginning with Niall Taro Ferguson’s evocative new work, Three Scenes from a Journey to Suo-Oshima, followed by the elegance and exuberance of Saint-Saëns’ Piano Quartet in Bb major, and culminating in the passionate romanticism of Dvořák’s Piano Quartet No. 2 in Eb major. Three composers, three musical destinations, and four musicians taking the scenic route through a world of color, bold contrasts and unexpected twists! Alsup Photo Exhibit William Alsup will share with you a selection of prints from more than fifty years developing his own black and white negatives and printing on silver gelatin in his own darkroom. A wonderfully irreverent pair of professional opera singers, contralto Sara Couden and soprano Kate Offer, will bring you to tears of joy and hilarity with their take on traditional Christmas songs — here’s their invitation: “Do you like Christmas carols? Aria Kidding Ruins Christmas! is strictly for folks who like their “wassail” with extra “assail.” No holiday tune is too sacred to stop singers Kate and Sara, along with collaborative pianist Daniel Lockert, from improving it for their own entertainment. articles.text: make. The violin, like Venus, emerged fully developed. And, like Venus, it was miraculous. This musical instrument was born fully developed almost exactly 500 years ago in Italy. Of course there were a few changes, but they were minor… virtually invisible to the untrained eye. As the violin developed internationally, each country added unique characteristics. But communication being as it is, information is shared internationally. The annual Violin Society of America convention this year proved my point. Violin construction is truly international. With its origin in Italy, it spread to every country in Europe…and now to every continent in the world. The convention was intended to share information. It included concerts, socializing, and competition. This year the convention was in the city of Cleveland. My son and I had the opportunity to eat in a great variety of restaurants. The city of Cleveland has become an international center. The first restaurant of note was billed as a Cleveland barbecue restaurant. Another outstanding restaurant was Lebanese. In addition, Cleveland boasts large Italian and Polish communities. One of the most delicious meals I had was a beautiful lettuce wedge salad. It was impressive both in taste and presentation. All you need to do is cut a head of lettuce horizontally and top it with bits of blue cheese and dressing, add some sliced tomatoes, and perhaps some bacon or other meat of similar type. That’s about it. As for the violin makers’ convention, there were hundreds of string instruments on display. A jury had the immensely difficult task of choosing winners in the categories of workmanship and tone. Our local violin shop, Ifshin Violins, enjoyed success in both categories. A violin concert proved my assertion that it is better to play the violin without a shoulder rest. The instrument just sounds better and the player can avoid problems like repetitive strain injury. Violin makers know how to have fun. One event was unique in the “fun department.” Groups of outstanding violin makers gathered around tables that were filled with (to put it mildly) piles of trash. Their task was to construct musical instruments out of this junk. And these instruments were required to make music! The luthiers had to be great inventors. Their task reminded me of one of the inventions of Thomas Edison. He specialized in electrical inventions, but curiously he was proudest of the phonograph. This invention had nothing to do with electricity. It was purely mechanical. Shortly after it was invented in 1877, the world declared the phonograph “the wonder of the age.” The miracle was on side A of the disc. On the flipside of the disc was another miracle. These were the musical instruments created by the finest violin makers of the world using junk and trash. It was a wonder that these musical “instruments” could make music at all. One of the fun events at the annual Violin Society of America convention is to have the top violin makers of the world construct a musical instrument out of trash. It is quite interesting what they construct. The miracle is that it actually can play music. The recent Violin Society of America convention in Cleveland featured fantastic musical instruments as far as the eye could see.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group says they walk “rain or shine”—a claim put to the test last Wednesday morning. A forecasted “atmospheric river” slammed the area Wednesday morning, right as the walk was scheduled to begin. Despite the ominous forecast, the group always walks to avoid morning uncertainty and last-minute emails. The plan was simple: show up at the Exedra and Large bioswale on Grand Avenue decide what to do. Six intrepid walkers assembled in the heavy rain: Alicia Rivera, Pat Keller, Sherry Jacobs, Bill Ahern, Ken Hubbert, and Dick Carter, decked out in gear ranging from Sherry’s heavyduty rain slicker to Ken’s optimistic desert hiking shorts. No dogs attended. The mood was upbeat and jovial, like kids ready to splash in puddles while everyone else stayed cozy at home. Due to the deluge, Matt Gerhardt’s scheduled “Steep and Scenic walk” was postponed to avoid slippery trails and steep climbs. Instead, the resilient walkers decided to embrace the weather and check out the city’s first bioswale at Fairview and Grand Avenues—a quick 2.5-mile round trip. However, Bill Ahern had walked to the Exedra through Piedmont Park and reported that Bushy Dell Creek was a sight to behold. Instead of heading straight for the bioswale, the group detoured behind the Exedra, past the quiet tot lot, to the stairs leading down to the creek. Bill was right: the rushing water in the creek was higher and faster than any of the group had ever seen. They admired the roaring torrent from different vantage points along the park trail and captured a lively group photo by the raging waters. Next, they headed down Magnolia Avenue toward the bioswale, passing the Community Pool and taking care to avoid slippery leaves and metal plates on the sidewalk. At Jerome Avenue, the group turned down toward the majestic redwood grove at the top of Fairview. As they turned the bend, they momentarily lost sight Bushy Dell Creek Wet walk at Bushy Dell Creek: Alicia Rivera, Pat Keller, Sherry Jacobs, Bill Ahern, Ken Hubbert, and Dick Carter.

articles.text: The culinary cognoscenti have proclaimed flavors of the Eastern Mediterranean are all the rage, and for good reason. These tasty spice and herb combinations are familiar, but with an exotic twist. The good news for us is there are numerous options to procure them for your home’s kitchen. I find it is easier to try out a few prepared spice blends when venturing into new flavor territory to learn what suits my taste buds. Inevitably after a few uses I start “doctoring” the blend – adding here, subtracting there, until I start making my own concoctions. Such is the case for ras el hanout, a spice blend originating in North Africa. It translates from Arabic to “top of the shop,” implying the best spices available go into the mix. While there are many versions (some with dozens of ingredients), most include cumin, ginger, cinnamon, cardamom, coriander, turmeric, cayenne, allspice, cloves, salt and pepper – spices found in most well-stocked pantries. You might notice these are also very warming spices – perfect for cold winter days. Starting with a prepared blend, this soup comes together very quickly, under 30 minutes. This recipe is perfect for adapting according to your tastes and what you have available. After all, it’s soup – so there’s a wide range to navigate! Experiment by switching out the kale for any winter green, and adding some shredded cooked chicken for a hearty meal-in-a-bowl. Advance Tip: Use fresh spices and herbs for optimal flavor. Purchase carefully, ideally procuring locally ground spices and herbs as most lose their peak flavor by about one year’s time. Store them in airtight containers in a cool, dry location. Butternut Squash, Chickpea and Kale Soup Ingredients • 1 tablespoon olive oil • 2 cups butternut squash, diced into ½-inch cubes • ½ cup onion, diced • 2 cloves garlic, minced • 1-2 teaspoons ras el hanout spice blend, to taste • ½ teaspoon ground cumin • 1⁄8 teaspoon cayenne pepper, or to taste • Salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste • 32 ounces chicken or vegetable broth, homemade or low sodium • 1½ cups cooked chickpeas, rinsed and drained (equals 1, 15-ounce can) • 3 cups kale leaves, remove the tough center stem and slice into ¼-inch ribbons • Greek yogurt and fresh cilantro leaves to serve, optional Instructions 1. Heat the olive oil in a large saucepan over medium heat until shimmering. Add the butternut squash, stirring occasionally, until the edges begin to brown and the squash begins to soften; about 4 minutes. Add the onions and stir frequently until they start to become translucent; about 2 minutes. 2. Add the garlic and spices, stirring constantly to evenly coat the squash and onions. Be careful to avoid scorching the garlic and spices. 3. Add the chickpeas and broth. Bring to a low boil. Add the kale and simmer until it is tender but retains a bright green color; about 4-5 minutes. Taste and adjust seasoning, salt and pepper accordingly. 4. Ladle the soup into serving bowls, garnish with a dollop of yogurt and freshly chopped cilantro and serve. Joaninha, a Piedmont resident and author, spent 12 years writing a book titled Recipes for a Good Life on the healthy recipes that she’s learned from her decades of experience traveling the world working as a wellness coach. Through the Piedmont Adult School, she decided to sign up to teach three cooking classes in the new year to teach residents about healthy eating and habits Joaninha found her passion for wellness and healthy cooking when she was a kid. At a young age, Joaninha would get sick often, going in and out of the hospital. At 14, she needed surgery that left her so weak she couldn’t return to school. She turned to her mother’s diet, health, and exercise books to rebuild her strength. Based on the books, she made her own health program and dietary plan that helped her regain her weight and return to school. After college, Joaninha worked as an artist and fashion designer; it wasn’t until around the late ’90s that she decided this career wasn’t for her. The isolating nature of an artist did not fit with her social personality, so she worked with a career coach to decide her future career path. The career coach recommended Joaninha work in a field with food. She agreed and, a few years later, moved to the south of France to teach cooking classes and become a consultant for health and wellness. “I started consulting with them on how to improve their diet, how to eat better, and how to relax. I did cooking classes and lady lunches for ladies. That’s when the idea of writing a book came, not from me, but from the people I worked with,” said Joaninha. With the idea of writing a book in her head, she attended a group seminar for female entrepreneurs where they all encouraged her to write a cookbook. “I wanted to make it very reader-friendly and simple so that somebody who really wants to improve their health but doesn’t cook much could pick up the book and say, ‘Oh, I can do this,’” said Joaninha. She would spend years reworking her recipes and manuscripts with a professional writer and editor before publishing the book with Regent Press in Berkeley. She’s spent the last few months attending book signings at local bookstores, meeting many people who want to improve their health. “I know what illness is about because I came from that place. There may be things you want to do, and you can’t do them because you have limitations because of poor health, and my feeling is that the most important thing is to work on your health because it not only makes you feel better but also gives you a good attitude,” said Joaninha. She has three classes for Spring 2027: one on healthy Valentine’s chocolate, the nutritional benefits of Indian food, and a presentation on eating for wellness and energy. More details on these classes can be found on the Piedmont Adult School’s website at https://adulted.piedmont. k12.ca.us/ under the Spring 2027 catalog. Registration for these classes will open December 11 at 9 a.m.

I think it is going to make it really hard for us to rebuild those Piedmont numbers if we’re not able to have enough hours or afford enough hours here to be the community partner that we were for 50-year-plus years,” said Shultz. Under the old arrangement, the team had a multi-year use agreement for the pool. Now, they are operating under a threemonth use agreement. According to Shultz, this new agreement structure makes it very difficult for them to plan for an entire season. According to Shultz, if PST does not regain its youth team multi-lane discount for next season, they may need to consider raising dues to accommodate the increased costs. PST is a nonprofit, year-round co-ed club for swimmers ages 6–18, run by a volunteer parent board and professional coaches. It has about 192 swimmers and offers competitive opportunities, including regional and national meets. After six years without a home pool, its swimmers and coaches have been spread across several East Bay facilities. Shultz feels like PST has become a second family for a lot of its swimmers. Many kids join the team very early in their lives. They grow with their coaches and friends, spending years together in the pool. This community was shown at the meeting, as many swimmers spoke during public comment to express their love for PST and the hope that the city will re-establish its relationship with the team. Junior team captain of PST Magnolia Stoll emphasized the impact this team has had on her life. “The team has become an incredibly important part of my life. Some of my closest friendships and meaningful memories have come from swimming. Having the team back at its hometown pool connects competitive swimming with the broader community and gives younger swimmers role models they can look up to,” said Stoll. The team is requesting longer-term agreements for pool usage, the reinstatement of the youth multi-lane discount, and a collaborative scheduling approach with other pool users to find a solution that benefits everyone. They aim to secure six lanes for their use on weekdays from 4 to 7 p.m. “This is the bare minimum we need for our swimmers and their training. Having this access will help us become a meaningful swim team in the community and provide an option for Piedmont families,” said Shultz. Commissioners did not respond to comments at the meeting, but Commissioner Sean Byrnes proposed a future agenda item to discuss “the right principles… for making these sorts of trade-off decisions.” He said it wouldn’t be about setting the schedule, but about guiding what the community’s priorities are when making these decisions. pages.text: 28 28 Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Cross Country Continued from page 12 For Schleuning, the close of his high school running career is a moment of perseverance. He battled ankylosing spondylitis, which caused him to miss his entire junior season. “I was out my entire junior year with a condition called ankylosing spondylitis. It’s a genetic condition, and basically it’s something that is wrong with my immune system. I had a stress reaction, which is the precursor to a stress fracture. I take injections now every week, and wasn’t able to get a summer block in of training. I had to adjust; everyone at the start of the season was a lot faster than me, and I just had to come at it with the understanding that I had room to grow throughout the season,” Schleuning said. Following Schleuning was sophomore Dylan Wallway, finishing 52nd in 17:11.3. Freshman Cormac Ross was 59th in 17:17.1, fellow freshman Jackson Chu was 64th in 17:29, while junior Luca LaForte was 82nd in 17:54.6. Looking ahead to next season, the girls’ team will be led by Oesterer but must fill in for the graduation of Mand, Gray, Brozowski-Schrader, and Thornton. They could still bring back an experienced group with Coleman, Ewen, junior Nikita Gorelik, and sophomore Camille Hauser. As for the boys, Schleuning will say his goodbyes, but the Highlanders boasted a young group through 2026. Next season could feature Wallway, Ross, Chu, LaForte, sophomore Blake Riif, and junior Dresden Schulte-Sasse. Viviane Oesterer finished 15th of 132 runners at the NCS Championship, coming one spot away from qualifying for State. Alex Schleuning led the boys’ team, wrapping up his PHS cross country career with a 29th of 168 finish at the NCS Championship.
